extracted.intended_audience: general readers and policymakers interested in postwar U.S. economic and regulatory actions
extracted.subtask_description: A news report describing post-World War II U.S. government measures (CPA, OPA, FTC, housing priorities) to control prices, allocate materials, and stabilize production in textiles, housing, food and other sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPA spindle-freeze order
rubrics_metrics.description: An order effective May 1 which 'freezes' for essential production the spindles turning out over 20 percent of the nation’s cotton yarn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restores wartime control dropped last August; spindles which produced certain yarns on Dec. 31, 1945, must be returned to manufacture of such yarns to check a 13 percent drop in yarn output and bolster supplies for clothing and other industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPA set-aside regulation to prevent diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A set-aside regulation intended to stem 'the serious diversion of yarn deliveries away from essential clothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to keep yarn supplies flowing to essential uses (inexpensive clothing and other critical goods) rather than to more expensive or nonessential fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five percent yarn price increase
rubrics_metrics.description: A five per cent increase in price ceilings for cotton yarn needed for low and moderately-priced garments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paired with yarn/fabric controls to support production of inexpensive clothing; part of a broader set of price adjustments by OPA and CPA to maintain supply while allowing modest price changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration of wartime fabric/material controls
rubrics_metrics.description: CPA restored wartime regulation which requires fabric/material allocation for inexpensive clothing; OPA at that time increased prices for cotton fabrics and later paralleled yarn price boosts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This action completes a cycle of controls governing all phases of cotton clothing production from yarn to finished garments to ensure materials are available for low-priced clothing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production output targets for yarn
rubrics_metrics.description: CPA expects output of yarn made for sale by manufacturers to increase from about 195,000,000 pounds to 235,000,000 pounds each quarter (target for the year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spindle freeze and allocation measures are justified as necessary to reverse a downward trend (13% drop) and avoid 'disastrous consequences' across textiles, clothing, tire, furniture and shoe manufacturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority allocation to essential end-uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Yarn freeze and set-aside aimed to provide fabrics for shorts, pajamas, dresses, work clothing, men's suits, hosiery, shoe fabrics, zipper tapes, furniture fabrics, webbings, fish nets, tire cord and other critical items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists many specific end-uses intended to receive priority; the policy ties spindle allocation back to these enumerated essential categories to justify restrictions on other uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housing price and rent ceilings for veteran housing program
rubrics_metrics.description: A priority order sets new and lower ceilings on prices and rents for at least half the new homes built in each city; new price limits are for the total costs of the finished house and vary city by city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some homes in each city's program may be sold for up to $10,000 or rented for up to $80 as before; the order is milder than wartime controls but may prompt more rigid wartime-type controls in lagging cities if targets are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of price ceilings to support housing goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal order establishes ceilings (examples mention ranges like $40 to $65 in some contexts and varying per city) to keep low-priced homes available for veterans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the order fails to produce enough low-priced homes, more stringent wartime-style controls may be applied to lagging cities; legislation and favorable circumstances are cited as prerequisites for holding the overall price line.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC concern about bread waste from consignment selling
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC charged that large quantities of bread were being wasted as a result of bakers' practice of taking unsold bread from retailers under the consignment selling arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights need to regulate consignment selling or monitor retail returns to prevent waste in the bread supply especially during periods of reduced production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of commodity price spikes if controls removed (corn example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government grain expert William McArthur testified that corn prices could 'go very high' (rumored up to $3 a bushel from about $1.20) if controls were eliminated; such a rise could force farmers to cut back livestock and poultry because they couldn't afford feed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as policy rationale for maintaining price controls to prevent sharp increases that would harm downstream agricultural production and food availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural right to be heard on administrative regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court ruled that persons protesting OPA regulations are entitled to be heard even though those regulations subsequently were changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms procedural fairness requirements when agencies issue or change price-control regulations; agencies should provide opportunities for hearings or protests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding purposes for continuing OPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration leaders argue OPA should be continued 'as is' to prevent inflation, maintain the price line, and keep production and supplies stable; opponents call some measures 'hokum' or overreaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate criteria include: preventing inflation, avoiding crippling amendments that would weaken OPA, balancing producer/distributor interests (e.g., fair pricing formulas), and ensuring speedy decisions on price adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested Price Administrator ceiling-establishment duty (Besse amendment idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Besse suggested that 'Whenever a new price regulation is promulgated . . . the Price Administrator shall establish ceil[ings] which will provide...' (intended to provide prices that reflect fair factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although text is incomplete, the principle is that new regulations should include explicit ceiling rules aimed at fairness and prevent guarantees of excessive profit; legislative language would define the ceiling formula.
